lead: Shearing cuts sheet metal along a closed line by driving a punch past a die. The same tool can make a hole, called punching, or cut a part, called blanking; the difference is which piece you keep. Clearance, the small gap per side between punch and die, decides whether the cut edge is clean or burred. Press shops use these operations for washers, brackets, enclosures and electrical laminations. The force calculation uses shear strength and cut perimeter, not area.
prereq: You need: 3.1 for sheet strain limits and Unit 2 for shear strength and plastic deformation.

blocks.text: Shearing is a sheet-metal cutting process. A punch, the male tool, moves down past a die, the female opening. The sheet between them is loaded in shear. When the shear stress reaches the ultimate shear strength τ of the sheet, the metal fractures along the tool edges. The cut-out piece is a blank. Clearance c is the gap between punch and die per side. It is kept small, often 5% to 10% of sheet thickness t per side. Soft aluminium may use about 5%; hard steel may need about 10%. Zero clearance is not used: it raises force and causes secondary shear. Shearing exists because it makes holes and flat parts fast, in one press stroke, with little material waste. A washer, a bracket, a fan cover and a motor lamination all begin as sheared blanks.

items: Place the strip on the die, with the punch above it.
Lower the punch; the sheet is compressed and then sheared.
At shear stress τ, a crack starts at the punch and die edges and meets.
The slug or blank separates and falls; the punch returns.

blocks.text: Punching and blanking use the same tool and the same cut. The difference is what you keep. In punching, also called piercing, the punch removes a slug. The sheet with the hole is the product; the slug is scrap. In blanking, the cut-out piece is the product; the surrounding strip is scrap. A 50 mm disc cut from a strip is a blank if you keep the disc. The same 50 mm punch makes a punching if you keep the strip and throw away the disc. Both are high-volume, low-cost operations.

items: Notching removes a small piece from the edge of a sheet.
Trimming cuts away excess edge left by an earlier operation.
Slitting cuts a sheet along a line, often with circular blades, to make narrower coils.
Shaving removes a thin layer from a cut edge to improve finish and size.

blocks.text: After shearing, the part may go to bending or deep drawing.

sections.h3: Clearance, force and the cut edge

blocks.text: The punch force depends on the cut perimeter, not the hole area.

blocks.where: F is peak punching force in N; τ is ultimate shear strength of the sheet in N/mm²; L is the total cut perimeter in mm; t is sheet thickness in mm.

blocks.text: A shear angle on the punch face starts the cut at one side. The peak force falls, but the punch travels farther, so the work done is nearly the same. This protects the press.

items: Rollover: a rounded top edge where the punch presses in.
Burnish: a smooth vertical band cut by plastic shear.
Fracture: a rough, angled zone where the metal tears.
Burr: a sharp lip at the bottom.

blocks.text: Correct clearance gives a clean burnish band, roughly one-third of thickness. Too little clearance causes secondary shear and a tall burr. Too much clearance causes heavy rollover, a rough fracture and a large burr.

figure.caption: The tree separates shearing by what you keep: punching keeps the sheet and scraps the slug, blanking keeps the cut blank and scraps the strip.

spec.aria: Tree separating shearing into punching, where the hole is scrap, and blanking, where the cut blank is the product.

examples.question: A 2.0 mm thick steel sheet is punched with a 50 mm diameter hole. The ultimate shear strength of the steel is 300 N/mm². Find the punching force in N and kN.
steps: Cut perimeter L = π × d = π × 50 mm = 157.0796 mm, which rounds to 157.1 mm.
Use the shearing force formula F = τ × L × t.
F = 94,247.8 N, which rounds to 94,248 N.
examples.answer: The punching force is about 94.2 kN, or 94,248 N.
examples.check:
import math
d = 50.0
t = 2.0
tau = 300.0
L = math.pi * d
F = tau * L * t
print(round(L, 1))
print(round(F))
print(round(F / 1000, 1))

traps: Using tensile strength in place of ultimate shear strength: the formula needs τ, the shear value.
Using hole area πd²/4 instead of cut perimeter times thickness, L × t.
Swapping punching and blanking: in punching the slug is scrap, in blanking the blank is product.
Treating clearance as a total gap: tables give clearance per side, as a percentage of thickness.
Forgetting that a shear angle lowers peak force, not the total shearing work; also keep N and kN consistent.

quiz.a: Blanking is a shearing operation in which the cut-out piece, the blank, is the required product and the surrounding strip is scrap.

quiz.q: Why is clearance provided between punch and die?
quiz.a: Clearance lets the metal fracture cleanly instead of being torn by secondary shear. It reduces punch force, controls the burnish band and limits burr. Zero clearance raises force and damages the edge.

quiz.q: A 1.5 mm sheet has a 30 mm diameter hole punched. τ = 250 N/mm². Find the punching force.
A punched hole shows heavy rollover, a rough fracture and a large burr. What is the likely cause and remedy?
quiz.a: Clearance is likely too large. Reduce clearance to the recommended 5% to 10% of thickness per side for that material, and check punch-die alignment.

quiz.q: In punching, which piece is scrap?
quiz.a: The punched slug is scrap; the sheet with the hole is the product.

quiz.q: What does a shear angle on the punch do to peak force and total work?
quiz.a: It reduces peak force because cutting starts at one side. Total work is nearly unchanged because the punch travels farther.

quiz.q: A cut has perimeter 200 mm in a 3 mm sheet with τ = 400 N/mm². Find the shearing force.
The same tool makes a hole in one job and a disc in another. Explain the difference.
quiz.a: The tool and cut are the same; the product decides the name. If the sheet with the hole is kept, the operation is punching and the slug is scrap. If the disc is kept, the operation is blanking and the strip is scrap.

beyond: Not for the exam. Fine blanking uses a counter-punch and a ring to clamp the sheet, giving a nearly vertical cut edge for gears and brake parts. Magnetic pulse shearing uses a pulsed electromagnetic coil to drive a flyer into the sheet at high speed, reducing burr in thin aluminium and copper. Servo presses can program punch speed through the stroke to cut noise and tool wear. Search terms: fine blanking, magnetic pulse shearing, servo press blanking, punch wear monitoring.
